utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in court. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my learned friends from the Prosecution, to all those in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Mr. Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Delic, with our assistant, Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much. Before we call -- before we call the witness in, just a small housekeeping matter. The Prosecution has filed some motions to lead evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, good, and it -- I think the first of those testifying is going to be sometime next week. I just wanted to find out from the Defence whether it's possible for you to come up with any response, so that an order can be given. I'm not suggesting you give that response now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. As yet we haven't seen the motion. We will have a look at it today and we will endeavour to respond as early as we can next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If I may just check with Mr. Mundis. Mr. Mundis, when is that -- if -- if that motion is not granted, then it has to come viva voce. When would he have to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. He's scheduled to appear one week from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One week from today. So it's Friday next week. Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Mr. Robson, I -- I understand that you haven't seen the motion. Can I put slight pressure on you to try and aim for Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll aim for Tuesday, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You'll aim for Tuesday. Thank you very much I'm most indulged to you. Having said that, Mr. Mundis, am I wrong to suggest that in fact your motion is out of time, in terms of our guidelines?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I can simply indicate that in light of the timing in which one of those -- or two of those statements were taken, being the 17th of September, that we've endeavoured to file as quickly as possible. We did have -- encounter some difficulties yesterday in filing with respect to the large size of the document. We were unable to file it electronically pursuant to the Registry's guidelines, and as a result we had to then file it in hard copy this morning. So I am aware of that, Your Honours, and we, as I've indicated, are endeavouring to do everything possible to ensure that the Trial Chamber has all of the relevant evidence and that the case is presented in the most expeditious way possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse my slow uptake. When you say those statements were taken on the 17th of September, what statements are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The statements which are annexed to the -- to the motion that was filed, consolidated statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I haven't read the -- the motion, so I haven't seen those statements. I'm just aware of the motion. Are these not statements that should have been taken much earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If this witness was lined up -- is this witness on the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. There are three -- three witnesses referred to in the motion. All three of them are on the 65 ter list. What we have proposed doing in the motion is seeking leave to move them from being viva voce witnesses to being 92 ter witnesses, number one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Number two, those witnesses were shown a number of exhibits that are on the exhibit list, and in the statements that are attached to the motion, there is a table with respect to two of them where the witness comments on the exhibits on the exhibit list. And what we have proposed doing is tendering the written statement and the exhibits which are explained or commented upon by the witness so that what we have proposed doing is, in effect, making additional time available to the Defence for cross-examination by foregoing a direct examination, which would include a direct examination covering a certain number of exhibits which are explained or commented upon by the -- by the witness in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Having heard what you've said, I -- I think the Chamber is still of the view that you should try to be punctual with your motions and you are -- you are given indulgence for now, but I think you will be put under pressure next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just state as well: As I stated earlier, we will aim to respond by Tuesday, but my heart does sink a little when I heard from the Prosecutor that they were unable to file the motion electronically due to its size. So we'll wait and see what we receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, let's wait and see what you -- do the best you can. Okay? Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. We will not tie you down to Tuesday, but if you can, please. May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, Mr. Robson, do you have something --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are waiting for the witness? Is he under cross-examination at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me put on the record, we are -- we are done with the -- with the direct examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just put it on the record. Thank you so much. Are we fetching the witness from ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You made a declaration at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I remind you that you are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth and nothing else but the truth. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm quite clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Prosecutor has finished asking his questions to you. It is now an opportunity for the Defence to ask you questions. Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Delic. My name is Nicholas Robson, and I'll be asking you some questions today on behalf of General Rasim Delic. If I could say at the outset that we've got many --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could say at the outset, we have many issues to get through today. I'd be very grateful if you could please focus on my questions. And if my question can be answered with a simple "yes" or "no," I'd encourage you to do so. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, yesterday you told us that from October 1994 you were the commander of the 2nd Corps of the ARBiH, is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The 2nd Corps had its headquarters in Tuzla, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, with regard to Tuzla, it's right to say that during the war that city was one of the most isolated parts of the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in your testimony, you explained the access to Tuzla via the main road and supply route from Zenica was cut off for most of the war. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the result of that was that the inhabitants of Tuzla were deprived of food and medicine for the majority of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in respect of Tuzla, it's correct, isn't it, that the United Nations designated that place as a safe area under a Security Council resolution?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, despite Tuzla having this United Nations safe area status, Tuzla was often targeted by Serb artillery, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the war, all the way through to the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. When was it so declared a safe area by the United Nations? Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was back in 1993, but I'm not sure. At that time Srebrenica, Zepa, and some other towns were designated as safe areas. I believe that there were four or five of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, using their artillery, Serb forces could fire on Tuzla from strategic positions on the Mount Ozren salient, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But they could do that from the Majevica positions as well. Practically from all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just in respect of the Mount Ozren Serb positions that, was approximately 20 kilometres away from Tuzla, is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around 20 kilometres. However, their artillery, such as 120-millimetre Howitzers and other pieces of artillery that they had at their weapons -- disposal, could fire freely. At one point in time, they were not 20 kilometres away. They were at the Vijenac feature, which is less than 10 kilometres away from Tuzla as the crow flies. That's the Lukavica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you for your detailed response, General, but perhaps if you could just focus on the questions that you're being asked. Now, is it right that a particularly egregious incident occurred on the 25th of May, 1995 when during one of these Serb artillery attacks a grenade landed in the centre of Tuzla old town?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the very centre, I believe that there were 71 dead and over 200 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness a document in connection with this incident. It's document D407. For the record, this is a document from UNPROFOR HQ sector north-east to Major General Rupert Smith and it's dated the 28th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, do you see the Bosnian translation of that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we briefly could just turn to pages 2 in the English and Bosnian versions just to confirm whom the document is from.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was signed by Mr. Hagrup Haukland, brigadier general, commander of sector north-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If we could turn back to the first page, please. General, would you agree that this letter is addressed to Major General Smith?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at point 1, we can see that it says: "Please find enclosed with this letter the final report concerning the circumstances and events surrounding the tragic shelling incident which took place on the evening of 25th of May, 1995 in the centre of the old part of Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This is the incident that we've just mentioned, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may assist you, I, too, received a report containing a complete analysis of this event. Perhaps the -- Their Honours have this report, but I do have it at home, both in English and Bosnian versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I don't think that will be necessary. If we can focus on the conclusions at point 2 on this page. This letter, which summarises the report's conclusions, says that -- that there were at least 195 casualties directly caused by the shelling incident, of which up to 72 people were killed. Is it correct that there were 195 -- at least 195 casualties from this shelling?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more. I said at the outset that as far as I knew there was -- there were 71 dead and more than 200 wounded. The casualties in total amounted to nearly 300 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, General, if we look at point (b), if you can just read that. Does (b) confirm the deaths and injuries were a direct result of one high explosive shell or grenade?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we can see that that shell or grenade impacted in the midst of a non-combatant civilian crowd of several hundred people, and that was on the evening of the 25th of May. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Let me just add this: Three of them landed while -- one of them landed in the centre; whereas, the two others landed some 150 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look at point (c), we can see that the weapons system from which the shell or grenade originated came from the Ozren salient at a distance of at least 20 kilometres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then finally, at point (d), is it right we can see that from the location of the shell's impact, the time it was fired, and the type of shell used, it demonstrated that the purpose of the shelling was to inflict maximum casualties on a non-combatant civilian population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, is it correct to say that this shelling incident on the 25th of May was in fact the most deadly shelling incident that occurred throughout the entire war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the events causing most victims in one day. Although, around 1.200 civilians were killed by shelling in the town. I'm not sure about the figure, but I believe it's roughly thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And that goes back to what you said earlier, that there was shelling from Serb artillery throughout the entire war.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, apart from the shelling that was experienced in the Tuzla area, is it correct that the situation in your area of responsibility became even worse following the terrible events that occurred in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that those events occurred in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Officially on the 10th and 11th of July through to the end of July, but such a situation continued to exist later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, please could I admit this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be Exhibit 416. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, turning now to the 2nd Corps, could you explain to the Trial Chamber what the ethnic composition was of the 2nd Corps during the war.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The composition of the 2nd Corps of the BH army during the war reflected the composition of the population, admittedly to a lesser degree. However, particularly interesting was the town of Tuzla, where the composition reflected the ethnic make-up of Prigrad [phoen], except for the 9th Muslim, where there were no Serbs or Muslims and which was formed in late August 1995, all the other units had at least several dozen or several hundred or even more. In one of our brigades, which is the 115th Zrinjski Brigade, which was part of the corps or, rather, of the operations group 5, was practically half/half. Half of them were Muslims, half of them were Croats. There were some other units, especially the Reconnaissance Sabotage unit, as the commander of the staff I had 10 to 20 Serbs too. The number went down in time, partly due to fighting, partly due to the situation; however, even after the war in the professional army of the 2nd Corps we had around 200 soldiers. I don't know the exact figure - who were Serbs and who signed the first professional contracts. I don't know what the situation is at present because on several occasions the Federation army was reduced and their numbers must have gone down too, consequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General. It's right to say, isn't it, that within the 2nd Corps command there were also Bosnians of non-Muslim ethnicity throughout the -- the war?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation wasn't clear. There were both Croats and Serbs. My chief of staff, Andjelko Makar, was a Croat by ethnicity. Therefore, there were Croats and Serbs in the corps command of the corps. Chief of security, Ante Pranjic, was also a Croat. Assistant commander for morale was a Croat too, Pejo Kovacevic and his brother, they were members of the 2nd Corps for a while as assistant commanders for morale. All these units were made up of both Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is quite difficult to react at present; however, the interpretation doesn't really reflect what the witness is saying. It's been three days now that the interpretation has been quite poor of what is being said in Bosnian. I cannot correct what I'm referring to because there are entire parts that are incorrect. I can only suggest that we take the tapes from yesterday and today and to match them. I would have to spring to my feet every time something like this happens, and it's too soon and something is really disturbing about the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that the questioning is done by your colleague, just write a note to him, let him ask a question to clarify what is not clear. But let me also try and clarify something. In your question, Mr. Robson, you talked of Bosnians -- or it is transcribed as Bosnians of non-Muslim ethnicity. Is it supposed to be non-Muslim religion perhaps? Is Muslim --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- I posed the question there with -- on purpose, with that meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, is being a Muslim -- is that an ethnic characteristic or is it a religious characteristic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I don't want to get into an area of evidence, but we've obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead. As long as you have seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that question again, because it seems -- my colleague informs me that the -- the response was not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, General, just to put that question to you again. Obviously I'm interested in the 2nd Corps command. Can you confirm for us that there were members of the command who were non-Muslims within the command?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if you could again just -- I'm sorry that you have to do this, but please could you explain to the Tribunal who those people were and what positions they held.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, and I hope I won't forget anyone. The first commander of the 2nd Corps was a Croat, Zeljko Knez. The chief of staff and later on my deputy was Andjelko Makar. Ante Pranjic was the chief of security, and later on he was the assistant commander for garrison affairs. Pejo Kovacevic and his brother were assistants for organisational and mobilisational issues and for morale. There were others, other commanding officers occupying lower positions, but these were my associates, my immediate assistants that spring to my mind at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, General, the names of the persons you just mentioned, Knez, Pranjic, Kovacevic, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber the ethnicity of those persons. And there was somebody else as well, which I don't think their name was perhaps captured.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pejo and Dragan Kovacevic, they were two brothers who were also there. Most -- most of them were Croats; although, there were Serbs among them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. So just to clarify, Pejo and Dragan Kovacevic were of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I believe they are Croats, but I never asked them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Zeljko Knez, can you say --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Croat, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Andjelko Makar? I think the --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Croat, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And Ante Pranjic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Pranjic is a Croat, I believe, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to discuss with you the right of members of the ARBiH to exercise religious beliefs. And if I could show you document P4068.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, this document is entitled "Provisional instructions on the organisation and functioning of religious life in the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, I see that the Bosnian version of this document is not particularly clear. Can you make out the -- the heading or the title of this document?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Provisional instructions on the organisation and functioning of religious life in the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Dated the 7th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you aware that there was an act that regulated exercise of religious beliefs within the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that from the beginning of the war, we allowed that. Huseinta Dragasovic [phoen], Captain Dragasovic allowed for that, and Catholics were able to practice their religious beliefs when they were not in combat. This existed throughout the war, and I believe it exists now, and this is the principle upon which the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina operates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, General, where you say "Catholics were able to practice their religious beliefs when they were not in combat," could you confirm that both Serbs and Croats could both practice their religious beliefs within the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said, both Serbs and Croats. Croats are Catholics, at least the majority of them, and Serbs were Orthodox. There was a room with a cross and all the other religious symbols. There was a guardian, a priest who went there to celebrate the mass. I have to say that they were in the same building but they had separate rooms set aside for that, two separate rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If I can refer you to Article 1 of this document. If you could try your best to read what it says.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps if I can read it out to you so you can receive an interpretation. It states: "During the period of martial law" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- shall we then get the English version on the screen so that we can read with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So Article 1 states: "During the period of martial law, in units, commands, staffs and institutions of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina (hereinafter: Armed forces) the free exercise of religious beliefs and performance of religious rites by the members of the armed forces is planned and organised." So my question, General, is: Do you agree that through these instructions, the free exercise of religious beliefs was planned and organised by the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I can agree with that, yes. Of course, to the extent that the persons involved wanted to and were able to exercise their beliefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, if I could refer you to Article -- if I could refer you to Article 2. You're -- you're probably unable to read this article as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely what I stated; although, the left part of the text is quite poor. This was allowed to all religious beliefs, to all soldiers. All of them had to be allowed and enabled to practice their religious beliefs insofar as the duty permitted. And at the end, it says that there has to be tolerance between soldiers of different beliefs in the ranks of the armed forces. I can't read the first two words in the sentence, and I'm talking about Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And that principle of tolerance between soldiers of different beliefs, that is reflected in what you described for us earlier when you informed us as to how it was in the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this document could please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 417. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In connection with this issue, could the witness please be shown document D394. Just to explain to the Trial Chamber, that this document is actually comprised of two separate documents that touch upon a -- a similar issue. If we could go to the first page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can read this out, this is an order written in Sarajevo on the 5th of April, 1994. It is the Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces, office of the commander. It is entitled "Marking a celebration of Orthodox Easter. Order." If you need a comment, I can provide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps just go to the bottom of that page, please. Could you tell us -- could you please tell us who it's from.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was signed by deputy commander Jovan Divjak. Brigadier General Jovan Divjak. And he's representing the commander -- rather, I can't see clearly whether he's representing the commander or he's the deputy commander. It is illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And I don't know if you've had time to -- to look at the document at all, General, but could you confirm for us that in this order General Divjak is ordering that a reception take place in order to mark the Orthodox Easter holiday? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. Even though I have never seen this document previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, can you tell us: In the 2nd Corps, did members of Serb ethnicity who held Orthodox -- the Orthodox faith, did they celebrate Orthodox Easter each year?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Easter. It's just one of the holidays. There was also Christmas and a lot of other religious and other holidays, celebrations of patron saints, and so on. As far as I know, all of them were celebrated, and on those days they did not go to the front. We tried to find another solution to accommodate them, to let them go to their home so that they could celebrate the holiday with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So that was the Serb members of the 2nd Corps. Did the same thing apply to Croat members who held the Catholic faith?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same applied. There was just a slight difference in their Easters and Christmases. I think it's just -- they were just one week apart, and they celebrated their holidays within that one week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If we can please turn to page 2 of this document. As I say, it's a -- it's a second order. And perhaps if General Delic could briefly tell us what -- what it is.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could the document please be enlarged. "Order to organise a reception for Catholic Christmas. Hereby submitted to General Staff and the headquarters of the General Staff." It says here on -- that this order is being issued on the basis of provisions on the instruction on organisation and functioning of religious life within the armed forces of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the signature, we can see that it is typed "Rasim Delic," but I would say that the signature is somebody else's, not his. And then it says how to organise this, the invitees, where they should be accommodated, invited, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that what it says is that it was signed for General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's right. This is not the handwriting of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could just finally confirm the -- the date of this document. Is it right that it's dated the 17th of December, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17th of December, 1995. Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, please could these -- this exhibit be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, I am not sure that the issue of religious tolerance was raised in the examination-in-chief. And given your objections as of yesterday, I'm curious to see where we are going with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you heard from the Prosecutor, yesterday or if -- perhaps the day before, they are presenting a case made up of many pieces, and each witness will come and tell one or two pieces of the puzzle. We will, of course, confront the issues that each of those witnesses deals with, and I will be coming to that shortly. But at the same time, we have a duty to put our case wherever we can. And General Delic here, as commander of the 2nd Corps, is, we would say, rather uniquely placed to deal with some of the other issues which are not -- have not been raised during examination-in-chief but have been dealt with by other witnesses. So it's an opportunity for us to introduce evidence on other very salient and important -- salient issues before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I very much appreciate what you say, Mr. -- Mr. Robson. And -- and I am mindful of the fact that the question of religion has cropped up previously. I'm mindful of that fact. What I -- what I don't understand now and I didn't understand then, when it first cropped up, is what -- of what relevance it is to the case. You know, that's -- that's my only problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an excellent comment, but it's a -- it's a matter that has arisen in the last few weeks. It's clearly -- it's something that the Prosecution has introduced. I share with you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it of importance to you -- to the defence of General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, we don't know what view you -- although you've indicated now, Your Honour -- prior to that, we didn't know what view you took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we take the attitude that we have to confront each and every --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that I'm taking any view. I'm aware it was raised, and I'm not fighting with you. I'm aware it was -- I was surprised that it was raised. I'm surprised it is being pursued, because I don't see it anywhere in the indictment, and I don't -- yeah, I don't see it anywhere in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, I don't think I have to say any words. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if you do know -- if you do know where the Prosecution is going with it and you are in a position therefore to -- to put your ducks in a row to defend your case on that issue, by all means go ahead. But just be advised that some of us on the Bench are lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what -- what I would say: I won't pursue this any further in front of the witness, but if it -- if the Trial Chamber wishes to air it, we would be very happy to deal with this at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Moving to another issue. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson. You may proceed. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think we got an exhibit number for the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, you had just asked for an exhibit number when -- the question was being raised. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 418. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm afraid -- sorry. For the record, I'm afraid that I will dissent on this. I find the document being not relevant, and so I would dissent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General Delic, turning to the issue of command and control within the ARBiH. It's right to say, isn't it, that at the start of the war the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina passed legislation which regulated the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, two laws were adopted: The Law on Defence and on Armed Forces. I don't know whether anything was adopted in the beginning of the war, and they set aside previous laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to show you Exhibit 9, which is the Decree Law on the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is it. While we're waiting for the English version to appear, General, could you take a look at the title of this document, and is this one of the laws that you just mentioned to us a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it is. This is the Decree Law on the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ejup Ganic signed it personally, he was deputy President of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was published in the Official Gazette, 3 -- 1335/92. And this was issued in Sarajevo on the 9th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, and that's just -- as to the issue of who it's issued by, if we could please look at page 9 of the English document and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear that then and during the entire war the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina served as the Supreme Command of the country and it was headed by the late Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Just taking it step by step, General, if we can look -- if you look at the right-hand column of this document, is it right to say that this law was issued by the Presidency -- President of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic? And it's just off the bottom of the English document there.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. 20th of May, 1992, President of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, signed it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could look at Article 8, which is on page 2 of the English version and page 1 of the B/C/S version. And you'll find it on the right-hand side of the B/C/S version. General, it's correct to say, isn't it, that we can see there Article 8 falls in a section entitled "Command and control of the army"?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says in that article what I said previously, that the Presidency of the Republic is the most senior organ in the command and control of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If I can refer you to Article 9. We don't have to move the screen. If you could read out for us the first -- the start of that article and the first three points, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 9, it says: "In achieving command and control of the Army, the Presidency of the Republic shall in particular:" Under 1: "Establish army development plans. "2: Establish the organisation of the army and formation of Army command, staffs, and institutions of the army. "3: Establish the composition of command and control in the Army in keeping with the law. "4: Follow implementation of the established policy principles and command and control of the army." "5: Establish the plan of use of the army in case of war and order the use of army in war and peace."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So would you agree with me, based on what you've just read out to the Trial Chamber, that not only does the law provide that the Presidency is the most senior organ in command and control of the army, it also sets up particular tasks and responsibility -- and responsibilities for the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in particular, the last point, 5, that you've just read out, that provides legal authorisation for the Presidency to order the use of the army during wartime, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was regulated by way of this item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we go back to the beginning of that Article 5 -- Article 9, without -- without losing subarticle 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe they're on two different pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are they? Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, did the last article - I'm interested in this law - is Article 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you like -- if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like them to go to Article 10 now in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you can turn to page 3, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down the page in the B/C/S version. If we can go a bit further in the B/C/S version, please. Thank you. And if we can just change that so we can see the entire section. Thanks. Now, Your Honours, there's a -- a translation error in the English version of this law, so I'll ask General Delic to read out Article 10, if I may. It's the top part and part 1 I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Article 9 or 10? Article 10: "President of the Presidency of the Republic shall, on behalf of the Presidency: "1. Representative the armed forces in the Republic and abroad. "2: Sign acts of the Presidency."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, based on that, would you agree with me that this article, 10.1, shows that the President of the Presidency was responsible for representing the armed forces, both inside and outside of the country?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. This was wartime and upon authorisation of the Presidency he was the one doing precisely that throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, you'll note that in Article 10.1, the words "inside" and "inside" [sic] are omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, turning to Article 10.2, is it right that that provides that the President shall sign Republic Presidency acts relating to the army and oversee their implementation?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the interpretation is not good. I have the Bosnian version here, and it says that the President signs the acts of the Presidency of the Republic which pertain to the army and he takes care of their implementation. This refers to the President of the Presidency, the late Alija Izetbegovic, who is authorised to sign the acts. He's authorised to do that on behalf of the Presidency -- the acts that pertain to the army and to take care of their implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify. By "acts," this could mean decisions, orders, or any other type of instruction relating to the army, is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This covers everything that pertains to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to put that exhibit to one side, if I may, and refer to some later legislation, which is document D401. Just for the record, this is a document entitled "Decision on the organisational chart of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. If -- are you familiar with this document at all, General?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing it, but I am familiar with this decision, with its contents, rather; although, I do not remember this document reaching me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could please look at page 6 of the English version and page 4 of the B/C/S version. If we could just -- General, could you confirm for us that this decision was issued on the 24th of October, 1994 and it was signed by President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you were familiar with its content. Is it right that this decision introduces a structure for the ARBiH that was in place until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could refer to page 2 in both the English and B/C/S versions, please. It's section 4 that I'm interested in. Exactly. Sorry, in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it Roman numeral 4 or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's Roman numeral 4 that I'm after, and I think we've got Roman numeral 5 in the B/C/S version. Is that -- is that correct? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, we can see there that the heading is "Organisation of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at part 1 of section 4, it states: "The Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall consist of: General Staff, air force and anti-aircraft defence command, six corps, Eastern Bosnia operations group-division. And then it goes on to say: "and three independent brigades." Could you first of all just clarify, what is the Eastern Bosnia operations group-division, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is in the area of Gorazde and that this should be a division which was created in the free territory; that is to say, Gorazde municipality and other liberated municipalities around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. The part we're interested is -- in is the reference to "six corps." And in that connection, if we could look at the next page, please, page 3 --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- of the English. And it's still page 2 of the B/C/S. If we could scroll down to the bottom of the B/C/S version, please. Okay. Now, would you agree with me, General, that part 5 of item 4 states: "The following shall be directly subordinated to and linked to the Army General Staff Commander." And then it goes on to say: "commanders of the units as referred to under item IV/1 of this decision."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that interpretation is not good. Item 5 defines this in different terms, and I will read it to you verbatim. Item 5 reads: "Commander of the general -- the following: Shall be directly subordinated and linked to the army General Staff commander, air force and anti-aircraft defence commander and commanders of the units as referred to under item IV/1 of this decision, deputy commander, chief of staff of the army," and then in parenthesis, it says "also," and then there's no more text following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page. If you can carry on, please, General.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, we -- I got no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And all administrations and departments listed in item IV/II of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you just repeat that last bit, General, just the first, the top part -- the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So and then it continues with this sentence: "Assistant commanders of the General Staff, the Army Staff, and all administrations and departments listed in item IV/2 of this decision. Administrations within the Army Staff ...."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, General, it is a little bit complicated, but from this part of item 4, we can gather the following: It says that commanders of the units referred to under item IV/1 of this decision shall be subordinated to or linked to the Army General Staff commander. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all clear to me. President and Supreme Command resubordinate what is within their jurisdiction to the commander of the General Staff. At least, that's how I read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And from this -- this law, could you tell us, who is directly subordinate, then, to the General Staff commander, General Delic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before General Delic answers, can I just ask that we -- we pause in between questions and answers, and can you also try to do that, General. The interpretation is not going at the same pace and some of us up here lose -- lose you if you go fast. Thank you very much. You may -- you may answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I took this to mean that the General Staff is the specialised organ of the Presidency and then the President of the Presidency resubordinated or transferred some responsibilities that fall within his jurisdiction and linked it directly to the General Staff. It pertains to these persons and these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, a little earlier on we read the text of section IV, IV part 1, and we saw that the units mentioned in there included the six different corps of the ARBiH. Do you remember? And perhaps we can get that back on -- on the screen. If we could go back a page.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely. Not only six corps. There was the Eastern Bosnian Division there; there were the three brigades, I believe that they were Sarajevo brigades; and another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Precisely so. But having told you that what I'm interested in is in the six different corps, would you agree with me that it follows from this decision that the commanders of those six different corps were directly subordinate to the Army General Staff commander?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the decision of the President of the Presidency, the decision subordinating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you would agree with me, then.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree that the effect of this decision is that the commander of the General Staff could only issue orders to the commanders of the corps and those other independent units specified in item IV/1 that we can see?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the units listed here, the corps and those units. I believe that there were assistant there -- assistants there or deputies mentioned there in command of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, General, you just referred to the corps and those units. Could you please specify what you mean by "those units."

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I meant the unit in Eastern Bosnia. I meant the two or three brigades mentioned herein. I believe that there were two or three brigades in Sarajevo. I'm referring to the units that were listed in the earlier paragraphs, because this refers back to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- first of all, if we could please admit the document into evidence. And I think it would be an appropriate time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 419. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General Delic, just before the break, we were talking about the decision on the organisational chart of the ARBiH. If I could just clear up a couple of points before we move on to the new -- on to a new topic. Could you confirm, General, that from that decision the consequence was that the General Staff commander could only issue orders to the commanders of those units listed in item IV/1? And we can bring that document back up, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need it. I think that you are quite right, except for representing them abroad, these units are enumerated. And you can see that in the relevant item.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So that means that the General Delic, the General Staff commander, could only issue orders to the commanders of the corps and those other units listed in -- that we discussed in the decision.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's also right to say, isn't it, that only a commander of a corps could issue orders to his subordinate units directly?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General. I'd like to move on to the issue of the directive that you mentioned yesterday in your evidence. If the witness could please be shown document -- or Exhibit 384.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to explain. You've seen this document before. And on the last occasion, we explained that we'd only managed to get a few small parts of the document translated. Unfortunately, the situation is still the same today, but we -- we should be able to manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, the document on the screen in front of you, is this the directive that you mentioned in your evidence for the year 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. On the 5th of January, 1995 the General Staff of the army, Kakanj command post, issues this to the command of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th Corps and the Gorazde Eastern Bosnia Operations Group. This is the directive for continuation of offensive combat operations by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then further below, you see the units and the tasks given to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please refer to page 9 in the Bosnian version only, just to see who the document is signed by.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is signed by the staff of the army, by Brigadier General Enver Hadzihasanovic. I think that at that command post he was the most senior officer and in charge of the duties of the chief of staff, and as such, he did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it right to say that General Delic approved this document? Can you see his signature?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. There's no signature here -- oh, just a minute. There is something underneath. I think that, yes, this is the signature of General Delic, although this is enlarged. It says: "Rasim Delic. Commander Rasim Delic." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And that's his approval.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could return back to the first page, please. Now, General, would you agree with me that -- you've mentioned a little bit about what this document contains, but it's right the first section deals with the forces opposing the ARBiH; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, information on the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn -- turn to page 7 of the Bosnian version and page 3 of the English, please. Is it possible to fit the -- it's points 5 and 6 that we're going to be discussing, so if they could be put on the page, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of this. There was also a map accompanying this document. I'm almost sure that there was a map. And in item 5, it says what the tasks of the 2nd Corps were. I said yesterday that these directives were more or less the same throughout the war. It says here that they should liberate the areas of Mount Majevica, Banj Brdo, Stolice, Busija Poversnica [phoen], Medvednje [phoen], Brusnice village and come out on the Priboj-Lopare-Celic road. In coordination with the 3rd Corps, liberate the general or the broader sector of the Vozuca. To cut off the Chetnik forces at Mount Ozren along the Klokotnica-Sevarlije axis. With the assistance of the other corps lift the blockade from the free territory of Srebrenica and Zepa and come out on the river Drina. So the tasks that were issued on a yearly basis. Actually, these were guidelines on what to do during the year, based on which commander of the corps commander planned his activities for the following year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you read out some of the tasks. Would you also confirm that in the last part of this section dealing with the 2nd Corps, related to lifting the blockade of Srebrenica and Zepa and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that the tasks set out for the 2nd Corps, liberating the general sector of Vozuca, lifting the blockade of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Sarajevo, these are all extremely general tasks?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All are quite general. It is very difficult to reach the state border and the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps included three and a half enemy corps: East Bosnia, 1st Krajina, Drina Corps, so basically the entire three corps of the enemy were located in the area of responsibility of this corps. These are general tasks, guidelines for some activities. The main goal was to maintain free territory and, if possible, reach the state border in the north and in the east: Drina -- the Drina River and the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the tasks set out in the directive constitute instructions at the strategic military level?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so. The strategic level was to reach the state border and liberate the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that the directive only defines the tasks for units at the corps level and it does not provide tasks to levels subordinate to the corps? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're completely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So based on the directive, it was the responsibility of the corps command to work out plans and issue tasks to the units subordinate to the corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. The corps was an independent unit which did not only within one year but within four years whatever it could, because there existed only guidelines and it was sometimes difficult to defend the territory, let alone to liberate it all the way up, say, to the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just for the purposes of clarity, when we talk about the levels subordinate to the corps level and, in particular, the 2nd Corps level, we're talking about the level of divisions and the autonomous units belonging to the 2nd Corps; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, going back to the events that you described at the early stage of your cross-examination in Tuzla and Srebrenica and Zepa, would you agree with me that it was militarily legitimate for tasks to be given to liberate the Vozuca sector and to lift the blockade of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite a logical question. I don't know if you're asking this for the record, but any child will tell you that this is logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If we can stay on the same page, and I'd like to refer you to the section below, section 6. Can you confirm that, again -- well, here we can see the tasks provided to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, within that section we can -- would you agree that the tasks are extremely broad?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer. It wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, could you please repeat that answer.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as in relation to the 2nd Corps. And I would say that in -- as far as I'm concerned, the task was even more ambitious -- or rather, the guidelines were even more ambitious. But I also had more forces at my disposal, but, nevertheless, I believed them to be overly ambitious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So just to go back to my question, what I asked you is: You would agree, then, that the tasks are extremely broad or general in nature?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could please look at page 4 of the English version and page 8 of the B/C/S. It's section 17 that we're interested in. General, would you agree with me that this section deals with security?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In item 17, in the first sentence, it says that: "The secrecy of implementation of decisions, orders regulating planning, preparation, and execution of combat activities is to be ensured and raised at a higher level." And then it says: "To provide counter-intelligence protection by way of organs of SVB," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can ask you, could you -- do you see the last part which deals with treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is in this directive as well. From 1992, the position was the same. The procedure with imprisoned persons is to be begun and completed with the military police organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please complete reading. The interpreters are -- do not have the written translation, so we're interpreting off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says underneath: "To the security, to the -- at the command post and forward command post is to be provided by way of a military police unit from the composition," and this is where the text ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'll do is I'll read out the English translation and if you could please let me know whether that accords with what you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Does it say: "Procedure with prisoners is to be started and completed with the military police organs engaging commanding officers from the military security and other trained organs as necessary"?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that here the commander of the General Staff was giving instructions to the corps -- the corps as to how prisoners of war should be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Based on the directive, it's right to say that the 2nd Corps extracted tasks and activities to be carried out at the level subordinate to the 2nd Corps; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I tried in the eastern part of the front to implement, with less success, with the 24th and 25th Division, to implement the plan around Majevica. And as for the plan concerning Vozuca, it has already been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right to say, isn't it, that as soon as the directive was issued, the corps was able to start work on planning combat activities based on the tasks contained in the directive?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you, because anything can be put down on paper; whereas, the situation in real life is something quite different. When I was able to found forces, resources, time, and ability, I began with implementation of the tasks. I told you that in the previous several directives the problem of Vozuca pocket was discussed, but they didn't manage to resolve it. Those were instructions and guidelines given to me based on which, given the forces, abilities, and resources I had, I tried to implement as much as I could, under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps at this stage we could look at Exhibit 401 in connection with what you've just told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document we saw yesterday. It's a plan entitled "Preparation of activities for combat operation, Uragan 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, General, we can see that the date of this plan is the 23rd of August, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can just go to page 3 in the English version and page 2 in the Bosnian. At the bottom of the page there, General, can you -- can you confirm that this plan was issued by you on that particular date?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, this is my plan. I have nothing to add or subtract. Everything that is stated here is so, and I can confirm that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And I think, as you said yesterday, this is a plan setting out the plans and activities in order to prepare for the operation Uragan; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that this plan shows what those tasks were, who was going to carry out the tasks, and the time frame for them to be completed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I explained this yesterday, that this was my plan - nobody needed to approve it - this was my activity. In order not to have to memorise what was going on and in order to have a proper order of tasks that needed to be performed and in order to assign tasks to certain people, I drew up this plan about how to implement the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If we could return to page 1 again, please. Now, General, if we could look at the top entry. It doesn't have a number next to it, but it's above the entry number 1. Do you agree with me that what that says is: "Drafting of the plan for combat operation 'Uragan 95'"?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Plan on activities for implementation of combat operation Uragan." This is what it says right in front of me. Perhaps we have different ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It may be that the interpretation is slightly different, but you have the correct box that I'm referring to. Would you agree with me, General, that next to what you've just read out it sets down the time frame for the activity to be completed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either your question or the interpretation is not clear. Something's wrong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise. We were -- we crossed wires at the moment. You have just read out the heading of the document, I believe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Plan of activities for implementation of combat operation Uragan 95."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. And if you look underneath there, we can see a table with a number -- five different columns. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is the number of activity, and then we have the activity, time, who executed it, and remark. Those are the columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at the second column, it has a heading that says "Activity." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Activity" is: "Drafting of the plan for -- of activities for implementation of combat operation Uragan 95." So the entire plan pertains to activities for implementation of combat operation Uragan, and the time frame for that is from the 16th until the 25th of August, 1995. Within that framework, the activity was to be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I see. So beneath where it says "drafting of the plan for combat operation 'Uragan 95'," those are all sub-activities [Realtime transcript read in error"Serb"] to be carried out by the corps command?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. We seem to not understand each other. Serbs have nothing to do with this. This plan was supposed to be produced by my staff, the staff of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Believe me, it's -- it wasn't what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, "sub-activities" was what I said, "sub-."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Let's move to a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Sub-activities. It's now corrected on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, General, I'll try and explore this a little further. The -- the first entry in the second column that says "drafting of the plan for combat operation 'Uragan 95'," underneath that we can find a number of different entries, 1, 2, 3, 4.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So all those numbered entries, would you agree with me that those are sub-activities or smaller tasks to be carried out in preparing the plan?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're quite right. All of this is an integral part of the activity that was aimed at producing the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, just going back to that very first entry in the second column, to the right of the entry we can see a time frame there, can't we? 16 to 25th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So is it right to say that the plan for the combat operation Uragan had to be completed within that time frame?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right, but only from the point of view of the corps command. Subordinated commands also had a certain period of time given to them to produce their own plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And on that point, if we could please look at page 4 in the English version and page 3, the B/C/S. Can you tell us what this document is, very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I remember. This is a plan that was postponed two or three times. Unfortunately, due to the 3rd Corps. Now, here it says: "Activities pursuant to the Uragan plan." It says: "Based on the readiness -- " I would rather say "non-readiness of the 3rd Corps units," but the text reads what it reads -- "which are conducting a coordinated action with our troops, according to the Uragan plan, I hereby." And then it says that the implementation -- it says: "I hereby order every activity planned to be carried out until the 26th of August, 1995, to be carried out by the 31st of August, 1995." "Item 2: All activity -- all activities planned to be carried out until the 1st of September, 1995, to be carried out by the 5th of September." That is to say, the deadline was extended because the 3rd Corps was not ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, General, you would agree with me that this order was given to the commands of the 21st, 22nd, 24th, and 25th Divisions on the 22nd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, and to be delivered personally to the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What this shows, then, is that you were ordering your subordinate units, the divisions, to prepare activities relating to Operation Uragan.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something I stated yesterday repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me, General, that this plan shows that you, as corps commander, as well with -- with your command were taking all the steps to plan Operation Uragan?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I was able to do, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown a different exhibit. It's 386.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a -- for the record, this is a document we looked at yesterday. It's an order from the General Staff at Kakanj dated 26th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you remember this document from yesterday, General?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And I can give you the following comment: Unless I am mistaken, unless I recall wrongly, I believe that this document was produced after the signing of that document for this operation. I believe this particular document was authored later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's exactly the -- the question that I was going to raise with you, General. So what this shows is that this document was sent from the General Staff at a point in time after the plan for combat operation Uragan had already been carried out -- sorry, had already been prepared.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the corps command is concerned, yes. However, the divisions had still been given enough time, although I believe that by that time they were ready too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's -- it's clear from the plan that we looked at a moment ago that it was up to the corps to decide which subordinate units to deploy in the combat operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's normal. I did not interfere with the decision of the division commander as to what he was going to do. I gave him the area, and within the area that he was given as part of his assignment, the division commander produced his own combat disposition and implemented the decision.
